s01: Each of these powers is ten times the previous one.
On a linear scale, the smallest almost disappear.
We can measure the number of multiplication steps instead.
Take one milliwatt as our reference.
Ten milliwatts is one factor of ten above it.
A hundred is two factors, and a thousand is three.
The base ten logarithm gives those exponents: zero, one, two, and three.
For power levels in decibels, multiply that exponent by ten.
The same four powers become zero, ten, twenty, and thirty decibels relative to our reference.
Equal steps now mean equal ratios, not equal amounts of power.
This also makes a chain of gains easier to combine.
Suppose one stage doubles the power, and the next multiplies it by five.
Together they multiply power by ten.
The first gain is about three point zero one decibels; the second, six point nine nine.
Their levels add to ten decibels.
Why addition?
A factor of ten to the power a, followed by ten to the power b, gives ten to the power a plus b.
Logarithms read those exponents, so multiplying ratios adds their logarithms.
Now reduce the power below the reference, to one tenth of a milliwatt.
Its level is negative ten decibels.
The power is still positive; the negative sign says below the reference.
A logarithmic scale keeps proportions visible across very different sizes.

scenes.narration:
Each of these powers is ten times the previous one. On a linear scale, the smallest almost disappear. We can measure the number of multiplication steps instead.

Take one milliwatt as our reference. Ten milliwatts is one factor of ten above it. A hundred is two factors, and a thousand is three. The base ten logarithm gives those exponents: zero, one, two, and three.

For power levels in decibels, multiply that exponent by ten. The same four powers become zero, ten, twenty, and thirty decibels relative to our reference. Equal steps now mean equal ratios, not equal amounts of power.

This also makes a chain of gains easier to combine. Suppose one stage doubles the power, and the next multiplies it by five. Together they multiply power by ten. The first gain is about three point zero one decibels; the second, six point nine nine. Their levels add to ten decibels.

Why addition? A factor of ten to the power a, followed by ten to the power b, gives ten to the power a plus b. Logarithms read those exponents, so multiplying ratios adds their logarithms.

Now reduce the power below the reference, to one tenth of a milliwatt. Its level is negative ten decibels. The power is still positive; the negative sign says below the reference. A logarithmic scale keeps proportions visible across very different sizes.
